probability-intro-s1.title: Rolling a red die and a blue die
probability-intro-s1.text: A red die and a blue die, both fair, are rolled. The grid lists the 36 equally likely outcomes as (red, blue). The shaded cells are the outcomes with a sum of 8.

probability-intro-s2.title: A club's members by class
probability-intro-s2.text: A club has 40 members: 12 freshmen, 10 sophomores, 8 juniors and 10 seniors. One member is chosen at random to win a prize. (Invented data.)

items.q: What is the probability that the sum of the two dice is 7?

why.correct: Six outcomes give a sum of 7: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1). With 36 equally likely outcomes, $P(\text{sum is } 7) = \frac{6}{36} \approx 0.167$.

mistakes.why: That treats the 11 possible sums (2 to 12) as equally likely. They are not: count outcomes in the grid of 36.
That counts (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4) but not their reverses. (6, 1) is a different outcome from (1, 6): the dice are different colors.

items.q: What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?

mistakes.why: That counts only part of the event: a sum of exactly 10 (3 outcomes), or only the sums above 10 (3 outcomes). "At least 10" means 10, 11 or 12, which is 6 outcomes.

items.q: What is the probability that the dice do NOT show the same number (not doubles)?

why.correct: There are 6 doubles, (1, 1) to (6, 6), so $P(\text{doubles}) = \frac{6}{36}$. By the complement rule, $P(\text{not doubles}) = 1 - \frac{6}{36} = \frac{30}{36}$.
options: Right: 1 minus the 6 doubles out of 36.
That is the probability of doubles, the complement of the event asked about.
That is the number of shaded outcomes (sum of 8), which has nothing to do with doubles.
That subtracts only (6, 6). There are 6 doubles, one in each row.

items.q: What is the probability that at least one of the dice shows a 6?

why.correct: The complement is "neither die shows a 6": $5 \times 5 = 25$ outcomes. So $P(\text{at least one } 6) = 1 - \frac{25}{36} = \frac{11}{36} \approx 0.306$. Counting directly: 6 in the red row, 6 in the blue column, but (6, 6) is in both, so 11.

mistakes.why: That counts (6, 6) twice, once for each die. It is one outcome, so there are 11.
That is the complement, neither die showing a 6.

items.q: A student says, "There are 11 possible sums, from 2 to 12, so the probability of a sum of 12 is $\frac{1}{11}$." What is wrong?

why.correct: Dividing by the number of outcomes works only for equally likely outcomes. The 36 pairs are equally likely; the 11 sums are not. Only (6, 6) gives 12, so $P(\text{sum is } 12) = \frac{1}{36}$.
options: A sum of 7 has 6 outcomes and a sum of 12 has 1, so they differ.
The number of possible sums is not the denominator; equally likely outcomes are.
Right: count equally likely outcomes, then divide.
(6, 6) has no different reverse; it is one outcome.
Nothing: each sum from 2 to 12 has the same chance of coming up
The answer should be $\frac{1}{12}$, because 12 is the largest sum
The sums are not equally likely; only 1 of the 36 equal outcomes gives 12
The answer should be $\frac{2}{36}$, for (6, 6) and its reverse

items.q: What is the probability that the winner is a junior?

why.correct: Each of the 40 members is equally likely to be chosen, and 8 are juniors: $\frac{8}{40} = 0.2$.

mistakes.why: That treats the 4 classes as equally likely. The classes have different sizes; count members instead.

items.q: What is the probability that the winner is not a freshman?

mistakes.why: That is the probability that the winner IS a freshman. Subtract it from 1.

items.q: Which gives the sample space for the winner's class, with the correct probabilities?

why.correct: The sample space lists every possible class. The probabilities come from the counts: $\frac{12}{40} = 0.3$, $\frac{10}{40} = 0.25$, $\frac{8}{40} = 0.2$, $\frac{10}{40} = 0.25$; they add to 1.
options: Four classes does not make them equally likely; the counts differ.
Right: each class's count over 40.
Those are counts. Probabilities are shares between 0 and 1.
These add to 0.95, not 1. Seniors are 10 of 40, which is 0.25.
Freshman 0.25, sophomore 0.25, junior 0.25, senior 0.25
Freshman 0.3, sophomore 0.25, junior 0.2, senior 0.25
Freshman 12, sophomore 10, junior 8, senior 10
Freshman 0.3, sophomore 0.25, junior 0.2, senior 0.2

items.q: Using the complement rule, write an expression for the probability that the winner is not a freshman.

why.correct: $P(F^c) = 1 - P(F)$ with F = "the winner is a freshman": $1 - \frac{12}{40} = 0.7$.

mistakes.why: That is the number of non-freshmen, 28, not a probability. The complement rule subtracts P(freshman) = 12/40 from 1.
That is P(freshman). The question asks for the complement, 1 minus this.

items.q: Which number could be a probability?

why.correct: A probability is between 0 and 1, inclusive. 0.85 fits; 1.2 and 105% are above 1 and −0.3 is below 0.
options: A probability is never more than 1.
A probability is never negative.
105% is 1.05, more than 1.
Right: between 0 and 1.

items.q: A forecast says the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What does this mean?

why.correct: A probability is a long-run share: over many days with conditions like tomorrow's, it rains on about 30% of them.
options: Right: probability as a long-run relative frequency.
The forecast is about whether it rains, not how long it rains.
The probability is about rain at a place, not the share of the area.
Unlikely is not impossible: it rains on about 3 days in 10 like this one.
On many days like tomorrow, it would rain on about 30% of them
It will rain for about 30% of the hours tomorrow, about 7 hours
It will rain in about 30% of the forecast area tomorrow, in some towns
It will not rain tomorrow, since 0.3 is less than half

items.q: A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability it is not blue?

why.correct: There are 10 equally likely marbles and 3 are blue, so $P(\text{not blue}) = 1 - \frac{3}{10} = 0.7$.

mistakes.why: That is P(blue). The question asks for its complement.
That treats the 3 colors as equally likely; there are 10 marbles, 7 of them not blue.

items.q: A soccer team can win, lose or tie a game. A fan says, "So the probability that we win is $\frac{1}{3}$." Why is the reasoning wrong?

why.correct: Counting outcomes gives a probability only when the outcomes are equally likely. A strong team wins far more than a third of its games.
options: Adding outcomes would not fix the reasoning; their chances still differ.
Wanting to win does not make a win certain.
Right: the rule "favorable over total" needs equally likely outcomes.
Two outcomes are also not equally likely here.
The sample space should also include a fourth outcome, a canceled game
The probability of a win is 1, since a team plays to win
Win, lose and tie need not be equally likely
The answer should be $\frac{1}{2}$, since a game is either won or not

items.q: A fair die is rolled once. Let A be the event "the roll is an even number." Which outcomes make up $A^c$?

why.correct: The sample space is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. A is 2, 4, 6, so its complement $A^c$ is every other outcome: 1, 3, 5.
options: Those are the outcomes in A.
That is the whole sample space.
5 is odd too, so it is in the complement.
Right: the outcomes not in A.
2, 4 and 6
1 and 3, the odd numbers below 4
1, 3 and 5

items.q: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?

why.correct: The sample space has 8 equally likely outcomes (HHH, HHT, ..., TTT). Only TTT has no head, so $P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - \frac{1}{8} = 0.875$.

mistakes.why: That is the probability of exactly one head. "At least one" includes 2 and 3 heads too.
That is the probability of no heads, the complement.
That is the probability of a head on one flip, not of at least one in 3 flips.

items.q: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

why.correct: An event and its complement together cover the sample space, so their probabilities add to 1, and so do the probabilities of the outcomes. A probability describes the long run, not any short series of trials.
options: Right: A and its complement cover every outcome, with no outcome in both.
Probability describes the long run. In 10 trials it may happen 3 or 7 times.
Right: one of the outcomes is sure to happen.
Not seeing it in 20 trials does not make it impossible.
$P(A) + P(A^c) = 1$ for any event A
An event with probability 0.5 happens exactly 5 times in each set of 10 trials
The probabilities of the outcomes in a sample space add to 1
An event that did not happen in 20 trials has probability 0
